summary: auth-service is genuinely self-saturated: CPU pinned at ~97%, worker pool saturating (active=64/64, queue=94198), accept queue full with 372x 503s on /v1/auth/login, and the autoscaler unable to help because desired replicas 14 exceeds maxReplicas 8 (F1-F6). The leading explanation — capacity saturation, i.e. login load outgrew provisioned auth-service capacity — is plausible but only low-confidence (0.45, below threshold), because the key discriminating metric, auth-service request_rate, was never retrieved, so we cannot yet show that incoming load actually rose before the sharp 06:52→06:54Z onset (F1). The reporter's bcrypt hypothesis is effectively ruled out: exactly one deployment landed across all services in the window and it was portfolio-service v4.4.0 at 05:50Z, with no auth-service release to carry a cost-factor change (F7, F13, F17). The secondary hypothesis (shared redis-cache perturbed by the portfolio-service release, ~62 min before onset) remains unproven and untested because no redis-cache or cross-service metrics were collected. Net: mitigation can start now, but the root cause is not adequately established.

ranked_hypotheses.title: Capacity saturation: login volume outgrew provisioned auth-service capacity (autoscaler capped at 8 replicas)
ranked_hypotheses.statement: auth-service request handling saturated its own worker pool and CPU because incoming login load exceeded provisioned capacity, and the autoscaler was capped at maxReplicas 8 so it could not add replicas. The result is CPU pinned at ~97%, active=64/64 workers, deep accept queue, and 503s on /v1/auth/login. No code or config change is required to explain it — the load/capacity relationship broke.

causal_chain.claim: Login request volume exceeds provisioned auth-service capacity (8 replicas worth of worker pool).
Worker pool saturates: active=64/64 with enormous queue (94198), CPU climbs to ~97%.
Autoscaler cannot add capacity: desired 14 replicas > maxReplicas 8.
Accept queue fills, requests rejected with 503 on POST /v1/auth/login; p99 climbs to ~3.8s and error rate to ~14%.

assumptions: Request rate actually rose before 06:52Z (request_rate was never retrieved for auth-service; this is the key missing metric).
The sharpness of the 06:52→06:54 onset could be a load spike crossing a capacity threshold, not a step change.

ranked_hypotheses.title: Shared-dependency perturbation: portfolio-service v4.4.0 (05:50Z) disturbed shared redis-cache, which auth-service depends on
ranked_hypotheses.statement: portfolio-service v4.4.0 deployed at 05:50Z is the only change that touches a component shared with auth-service (redis-cache). The new release perturbed the shared cache (e.g. key churn/eviction or a hot-key pattern), which propagated to auth-service and drove its per-request work up until its worker pool saturated and it self-throttled with 503s.

causal_chain.claim: portfolio-service v4.4.0 lands at 05:50Z ('Holdings export'), the only deployment in the window.
redis-cache is the single shared component touched by both auth-service and portfolio-service.
The new release degrades redis-cache behavior (eviction/latency/hot keys), slowing auth-service per-request work.
auth-service worker pool saturates and CPU pins, producing 3.8s p99 and 503s on /v1/auth/login.

assumptions: redis-cache was actually degraded by the portfolio-service release (no cache metrics were retrieved).
The degradation mechanism is CPU-bound rather than I/O-waiting: auth-service shows ~97% CPU with no connection-pool or dependency-timeout errors.

ranked_hypotheses.title: bcrypt cost/hashing regression from an auth-service release (reporter's hypothesis)
ranked_hypotheses.statement: A recent auth-service release reintroduced the bcrypt cost-factor regression (HIST-101), making /v1/auth/login CPU-bound, driving CPU to ~97%, saturating workers, and producing ~4s p99 and 503s.

causal_chain.claim: An auth-service release raising bcrypt cost factor lands shortly before onset.
CPU-bound hashing per login drives auth-service CPU to ~97%.
Worker pool saturates; accept queue fills; 503s and 3.8s p99 on /v1/auth/login.

assumptions: An auth-service deployment existed but was missed by the deployment queries.
ranked_hypotheses.rejection_reason: F7 and F13 (independently re-verified) show exactly ONE deployment across all services in the window — portfolio-service v4.4.0 — with no auth-service release. F17 confirms the HIST-101 precedent's mechanism requires a specific auth-service release that does not exist here. Signature similarity alone is not a trigger.

ranked_hypotheses.title: auth-service log.level config change (03:40Z) as origin of degradation
ranked_hypotheses.statement: The auth-service log.level INFO->WARN config change at 03:40Z altered runtime behavior or logging paths in a way that degraded /v1/auth/login handling, causing CPU saturation and 503s.

causal_chain.claim: Verbosity change somehow shifts work onto the login hot path.
auth-service CPU pins, workers saturate, 503s on login.

assumptions: A logging-verbosity flag could plausibly alter CPU-bound login hashing cost.
ranked_hypotheses.rejection_reason: F14/F16: the change is ~3.2h before onset and changes only logging verbosity; a 3.2h quiet gap plus no mechanism by which lower verbosity raises CPU makes this implausible. It may, however, have reduced diagnostic logs.

auth-service error_rate rose in the same 06:50Z bucket from ~0.2% baseline to 7.11% avg (max 14.76%), holding ~14% through 08:50Z.
The auth-service autoscaler could not relieve load: 34x WARN 'desired replicas 14 exceeds maxReplicas 8; cannot scale further' (first_seen 06:57:15Z), so horizontal scaling was capped at 8 replicas.

No evidence of connection-pool or dependency exhaustion in auth-service: connection-pool logs stayed 'healthy' up to 06:36:19Z (last such line before onset) and pre-onset logs contain no ERROR entries.

No auth-service deployment exists in the window, so the auth-service symptoms were not preceded by an auth-service release of its own.

recommended_actions.action: Raise or remove the auth-service autoscaler cap (currently maxReplicas=8) so the deployment can reach the desired replica count of ~14, then watch whether latency/error_rate recover.
recommended_actions.rationale: The autoscaler explicitly wanted 14 replicas but was blocked at maxReplicas 8 (F5). This is the single safe, reversible lever that directly addresses the observed saturation, and its outcome is itself diagnostic: recovery under added capacity confirms a capacity-bound incident, while no improvement points to a per-request cost change or dependency slowdown.

recommended_actions.action: Pull auth-service request_rate and memory_pct for 05:00-09:00Z (the missing metrics) and compare them against the 06:52->06:54Z onset.
recommended_actions.rationale: The capacity-saturation hypothesis (H1) rests entirely on the unverified premise that inbound login load rose. A rising request_rate before 06:50Z corroborates H1; an unchanged or falling rate while CPU and per-request work rise points away from pure capacity and toward a code/dependency trigger.

recommended_actions.action: Pull redis-cache metrics (CPU, memory, hit-rate, evictions, latency) alongside metrics for other redis-cache consumers (pricing-engine, market-data-service, order-service) for 05:30-09:00Z.
recommended_actions.rationale: The only change touching a component shared with auth-service is portfolio-service v4.4.0 at 05:50Z, and redis-cache is the sole shared component (F15); H2 cannot be confirmed or refuted without cache metrics. If other consumers are simultaneously degraded, H2 strengthens; if only auth-service is affected, it weakens.

recommended_actions.action: Retrieve api-gateway metrics (cpu_pct, error_rate, latency_p99_ms, memory_pct, request_rate, restarts) and per-route request counts for /v1/auth/login for the same window.
recommended_actions.rationale: api-gateway is the only caller of auth-service (F11) and is where a login-load spike would originate; its request_rate and error_rate distinguish 'real load increase' from 'auth-service got slower per request', which is the crux between H1 and a hidden per-request regression.

recommended_actions.action: Add an alert on auth-service autoscaler 'desired > maxReplicas' and on worker-pool saturation / accept-queue-full, and review the maxReplicas setting against peak login volume quarterly.
recommended_actions.rationale: The autoscaler cap warning fired 34 times (F5) yet the incident was reported by a human; an explicit alert on cap-hits and accept-queue-full would cut detection time. The HIST-113 precedent (capacity saturation resolved by raising replicas) shows this is a recurring failure mode.

recommended_actions.action: Establish a headroom/load-shedding policy for auth-service: load shedding with a clear 429/503 contract and pre-agreed replica ceiling for login storms.
recommended_actions.rationale: auth-service rejected requests with 503 only after the accept queue filled (F3); a deliberate load-shedding contract with correct status codes and retry hints would reduce client-visible failures during future capacity crossings.

recommended_actions.action: Re-examine whether any change or infra event is missing from the tracked change record around 06:19-06:54Z, including the unexplained 06:19:11Z 'slow request 3759ms on /internal/metrics' warning.
recommended_actions.rationale: No deployment or config change falls inside the 06:52-06:54Z onset window (F16), and the 06:19Z warning shares the exact 3759ms value seen post-onset, so either the true start is earlier or a change is untracked. Resolving this is required before declaring a root cause.

recommended_actions.action: Once a root cause is fixed, restore auth-service log verbosity (log.level WARN->INFO at least around login paths) and set a permanent floor for error/503 logging, since the 03:40Z verbosity reduction cost diagnostic evidence.
recommended_actions.rationale: The only config change in the window lowered auth-service log verbosity ~3.4h before onset (F9, F14), which reduced the log detail available for diagnosis; a verbosity floor preserves signal without restoring full noise.

recommended_actions.action: Add autoscaling-capacity review and per-service load forecasting to the change/tuning process, with headroom targets validated against observed peak login rates before any release.
recommended_actions.rationale: H1 and the HIST-113 precedent both describe capacity being outgrown without any code change (F18); a forecasting and headroom review prevents recurrence of the capped-autoscaler pattern.

recommended_actions.action: Make shared components (redis-cache) first-class with ownership and change-impact review: any release touching a shared cache requires a cache-metrics canary and a consumer-impact check.
recommended_actions.rationale: H2's unresolved question is whether a portfolio-service release perturbed the shared redis-cache that auth-service depends on (F15); a shared-component change process would prevent and quickly detect cross-service blast radius.

recommended_actions.action: Instrument per-request cost (e.g. password-hash CPU time) in auth-service so a future bcrypt-style regression is distinguishable from capacity saturation within minutes.
recommended_actions.rationale: This incident was initially mistaken for the HIST-101 bcrypt regression (F12, F17); the two causes produce near-identical latency/CPU/503 signatures, so per-request cost instrumentation is the definitive discriminator.
